articles.title: Powerball rolls again as three tickets share Lotto's top prize
articles.summary: Draw 2617 produced three First Division Lotto winners taking $333,333 each, but Powerball went unstruck for another draw, carrying its prize pool past $25.4 million.
articles.body:
Three Lotto tickets shared First Division in Wednesday night's draw, while Powerball went unclaimed for a further draw and Strike also rolled over.

The result

Lotto draw 2617 was made on Wednesday 2 September 2026 at 8:20pm. The winning line was 4, 8, 22, 25, 32 and 38, with 34 drawn as the bonus ball. The Powerball number was 3, and the Strike sequence came out as 32, 38, 4, 25.

Three tickets matched all six main numbers, splitting a First Division pool of $999,999 for $333,333 each. No ticket held the Powerball number alongside a First Division line, so the Powerball top prize rolled over.

Where the money went

The full Lotto division breakdown for the draw:

Lotto draw 2617 prize divisions
DivisionWinnersPrize each
One3$333,333
Two23$14,093
Three548$587
Four1,311$56
Five20,634$31
Six27,179$23
Seven289,391Bonus ticket

In total the Lotto pool paid out $3,794,295.80 across 339,089 winning tickets. Counting Powerball and Strike alongside it, the draw returned $4,755,270.80 to 480,746 tickets in all.

Powerball and Strike both roll

Powerball's First Division found no winner, leaving its prize pool sitting at $25,492,796. The game still paid out across its lower divisions, distributing $492,796 — four tickets took Second Division at $5,537 each, rising to a combined $19,630 when their Lotto winnings were included.

Strike also went unstruck at the top. Strike Four produced no winner from a pool of $668,179, though 77 tickets landed Strike Three for $707 apiece and 4,223 took Strike Two at $72. Across all Strike divisions, 113,984 tickets won something.

Reading the numbers

A shared First Division is not unusual. Lotto's top division is won by matching six numbers from 40, and when multiple tickets carry the same line the prize is split between them — which is why three winners here took a third each rather than the full pool.

Powerball works differently, and is why the headline figure keeps climbing. It requires a First Division Lotto line plus the separately drawn Powerball number, so it is struck far less often. Each draw without a winner carries the pool forward.

Worth noting for anyone reading a rolling jackpot as a signal: a larger pool does not improve the chance of winning it. The odds on any given line are unchanged from one draw to the next, whatever the prize has grown to.

The scale of the lower divisions is easy to overlook next to a seven-figure headline. Division Seven alone returned a bonus ticket to 289,391 entries — more than five in six of all winning tickets in the draw — while the three First Division winners represent a vanishingly small fraction of the 480,746 tickets that won something across the three games.

Next draw

Lotto, Powerball and Strike are drawn on Wednesday and Saturday evenings at 8:20pm. The next draw, number 2618, takes place on Saturday 5 September 2026. Entries close shortly before the draw — check with the operator for the exact cut-off.

articles.title: Bullseye top prize rolls over after 835391 draw
articles.summary: Friday's Bullseye draw produced no First Division winner, leaving a prize pool of $263,857 to carry forward. A single ticket took Third Division for $1,272.
articles.body:
Bullseye's top prize went unclaimed on Friday evening, with the drawn number landing outside every First Division entry and the pool rolling into the next draw.

The result

Bullseye draw 6155 was made on Friday 5 September 2026 at 6:02pm. The winning number was 835391.

No ticket matched it exactly, so First Division rolled over with a prize pool of $263,857 carried forward.

The divisions

Bullseye pays on how close a ticket sits to the drawn number, with each division covering a progressively wider band around it:

Bullseye draw 6155 prize divisions
DivisionWinning rangeWinnersPrize each
One8353910Rollover
Two835386–8353960$10,000
Three835341–8354411$1,272
Four834891–83589115$169
Five830391–840391167$38
Six785391–8853911,852Bonus ticket

A single ticket fell within the Third Division band for $1,272, the largest cash prize paid on the night. Second Division, which requires landing within five either side of the drawn number, found no winner.

In total the draw paid $13,857 across 2,035 winning tickets, with the balance of the pool carried forward.

What rolls over, and what does not

The $263,857 figure is the First Division prize pool, not the amount paid out on the night. Of the money attached to draw 6155, $13,857 went to winning tickets across the lower divisions; the balance stays with the top prize and carries into the following draw.

That distinction matters when reading a rollover. The pool figure quoted after a draw is what a First Division winner would stand to take at that point, and it grows each time the exact number goes unmatched. It is not money that has gone unpaid to anyone else — the lower divisions settled normally.

How Bullseye differs

Bullseye is structured unlike the rest of the Lotto New Zealand range. Where Lotto and Keno ask players to match a set of numbers drawn from a pool, Bullseye draws a single six-digit number and pays on proximity to it.

That produces the widening bands above: an exact match takes the top prize, while progressively looser matches pay smaller amounts. It also means the number of winners in the lower divisions stays relatively steady from draw to draw, since those bands cover a fixed spread either side of whatever is drawn.

The consequence for the top prize is that it is struck infrequently — a single specific six-digit number is a narrow target — and so the First Division pool builds across draws in the same way Powerball's does.

It also produces a very different winner profile from the rest of the range. Draw 6155 returned money to 2,035 tickets, the overwhelming majority of them in Division Six — a band ten thousand wide either side of the drawn number, paying a bonus ticket rather than cash. Only sixteen tickets took a cash prize above $38.

Next draw

Bullseye is drawn daily at around 6pm New Zealand time. The next draw, number 6156, follows on Saturday 6 September 2026, with the First Division pool carried forward from Friday.

articles.title: Keno draw carries a x10 multiplier for only the third time in 223 draws
articles.summary: Friday evening's Keno draw was attached to the game's largest multiplier. Our own archive of 223 consecutive draws puts that at 1.3 percent of the time.
articles.body:
Friday evening's Keno draw carried a ×10 multiplier — the largest the New Zealand game applies, and one we have recorded only three times across the 223 consecutive draws in our archive.

The result

Keno draw 27711 was made on Friday 5 September 2026 at 6:01pm. The twenty numbers drawn were:

1, 4, 8, 14, 21, 32, 33, 35, 40, 43, 45, 46, 51, 52, 54, 56, 59, 63, 65 and 80.

The draw carried a ×10 multiplier, meaning prizes on winning tickets for that draw were scaled by ten.

How rare that is

We hold every Keno draw from 12 July 2026 onward — 223 consecutive draws at the time of writing. Sorted by multiplier, they fall out like this:

Observed Keno multiplier frequency across 223 draws
MultiplierDrawsShare
×1.512154.3%
×26830.5%
×3219.4%
×5104.5%
×1031.3%

Draw 27711 is the third ×10 we have recorded. The others were draw 27676 on 28 August and draw 27601 on 9 August — 35 draws separated the two most recent, or roughly nine days at four draws a day.

These are observed counts from a limited window, not a published schedule. Lotto New Zealand set the underlying weightings, and a larger sample would shift the percentages. The shape is indicative rather than exact.

The draw itself

Setting the multiplier aside, draw 27711 was unremarkable, which is the usual state of affairs. Its twenty numbers summed to 802 against a theoretical average of 810, and split ten odd to ten even — exactly the expected balance. Both figures sit within ordinary variation, as they have across our full archive, where the mean sum runs to 809 and the mean odd count to 10.1.

Five of the twenty fell in the 50s, the heaviest concentration in any single band, while the 70s produced none at all. Clusters and gaps of that size are routine when twenty numbers are drawn from eighty and carry no significance for what follows.

What the multiplier does, and what it does not

The multiplier is selected before each draw and applies to everyone playing it. If a ticket wins, the prize for its tier is multiplied accordingly — so a win on Friday's draw paid ten times what the same result would have paid on a ×1 draw.

What it does not do is change the chance of winning. The probability of matching numbers is fixed by the rules of the game: twenty numbers drawn from eighty, with the odds determined entirely by how many spots a player chooses. Those odds were identical on Friday's ×10 draw and on the ×1.5 draw that preceded it.

Nor is it predictable. The multiplier attached to the next draw is unaffected by recent ones, and a long run without a ×10 does not make one more likely. Because it is drawn before any outcome is known and applies to every ticket in that draw equally, there is also no way to select for it.

Next draw

Keno is drawn four times daily at 10:01am, 1:01pm, 3:01pm and 6:01pm New Zealand time. The next draw follows on Saturday 6 September 2026 at 10:01am, with its own multiplier applied.
